municipalities.population_change_2012_pc.plain: How much the survey's estimate of the population changed from the 2008-2012 window to the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent.
municipalities.population_change_2012_pc.plain_es: Cuánto cambió el estimado de población de la encuesta desde la ventana 2008-2012 hasta la más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), en por ciento.
municipalities.population_change_2012_pc.definition: (total population in the latest window minus total population in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both are table B01003 (total population), cell 001, of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates.
municipalities.population_change_2012_pc.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), with B01003 cell 001 for the latest window and for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
municipalities.population_change_2012_pc.how_to_read: A negative value means the survey estimates fewer residents than in 2008-2012. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all municipalities but one (Rincón, +1.3%) show a decline. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B01003, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: It compares two five-year survey windows, not two census counts. For census-to-census change (2010 to 2020) use 'Population change, 2010 to 2020 (%)'; for yearly estimates see 'Resident population' in the Housing page series.

The Census Bureau sets the survey's population totals to agree with its own population estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) it published no margin of error for total population in 76 of 78 municipalities.

The Census Bureau's own population estimates were built on the 2010 census before 2020 and on the 2020 census from 2020 on, and the Housing page's population series steps up in 2020 for that reason. The survey totals are set to the Census Bureau's estimates, and this change spans the two bases, so part of it may reflect that break rather than people moving. The observatory does not measure how much.

commuting.daytime_change_pct.plain: How much a working day adds to, or takes from, the people in each municipio, as a percent of its residents.
commuting.daytime_change_pct.plain_es: Cuánto suma o resta un día de trabajo a las personas que hay en cada municipio, como por ciento de sus residentes.
commuting.daytime_change_pct.definition: Workers who come in to work minus workers who leave to work elsewhere, divided by the residents of the municipio in the 2020 Census, in percent. Above zero the municipio has more people by day than residents; below zero it has fewer.
commuting.daytime_change_pct.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 (workers 16 and over by the municipio where they live and the one where they work, each flow with a margin of error) and the residents of each municipio in the 2020 Census (geo/crosswalk.json). The workers who come in (from another municipio or from outside Puerto Rico) minus the workers who leave (to another municipio or outside Puerto Rico) are divided by the residents. Margins of error are at 90 percent: the margin of a sum of flows is the square root of the sum of the squares of their margins, and the census count has none. It is a calculated figure (decision 107): arithmetic on published figures, with nothing assumed.
commuting.daytime_change_pct.how_to_read: It is highest in San Juan (+31.7%), Guaynabo (+22.7%) and Cataño (+20.1%), and lowest in Toa Alta (-31.4%), Trujillo Alto (-22.3%) and Loíza (-20.8%). For 72 of the 78 municipios the change is larger than its margin of error, so its direction is clear. The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 38 of the 78 municipalities; in 35 of them the change is under 10 points, small enough for the margin to be a large part of it.
caveats: A value close to zero with a wide margin does not say whether the municipio fills or empties: read the margin.
It counts workers only, and one workplace for each worker.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020 and the residents are those of 2020.
commuting.daytime_change_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows, ACS 2016-2020, Table 1; 2020 Census residents by municipio.

commuting.daytime_population.plain: How many people are in each municipio on a working day: its residents, plus the workers who come in, minus the workers who leave.
commuting.daytime_population.plain_es: Cuántas personas hay en cada municipio en un día de trabajo: sus residentes, más las personas que llegan a trabajar, menos las que salen a trabajar.
commuting.daytime_population.definition: The residents of the municipio in the 2020 Census, plus the workers who work in it and live elsewhere, minus the workers who live in it and work elsewhere. The Census Bureau calls it the commuter-adjusted population.
commuting.daytime_population.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 (workers 16 and over by the municipio where they live and the one where they work, each flow with a margin of error) and the residents of each municipio in the 2020 Census (geo/crosswalk.json). Workers who come in are those who live in another municipio or outside Puerto Rico and work in the municipio; workers who leave are those who live in it and work in another municipio or outside Puerto Rico. The Census Bureau's formula is the resident population, plus the workers working in the area, minus the workers living in the area, which gives the same number. Margins of error are at 90 percent: the margin of a sum of flows is the square root of the sum of the squares of their margins, and the census count has none. It is a calculated figure (decision 107): arithmetic on published figures, with nothing assumed.
commuting.daytime_population.how_to_read: San Juan has 342,259 residents and about 450,689 people on a working day (margin ±3,342). 20 of the 78 municipios have more people by day than residents and 58 have fewer. The municipios add up to Puerto Rico's 3,285,077: the island loses the 2,657 workers who work outside it and gains the 1,860 who live outside it.
caveats: It counts workers only. Students, shoppers, patients and visitors also move by day and are not in it.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020 and the residents are those of 2020: the two periods are not the same, and remote work has changed since.
A worker is counted at one workplace, the one where they worked most in the survey's reference week.
commuting.daytime_population.source_detail: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows, ACS 2016-2020, Table 1, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/metro-micro/2020/commuting-flows-2020/table1.xlsx; 2020 Census residents by municipio. The formula: US Census Bureau, Calculating Commuter-Adjusted Population Estimates, https://www.census.gov/topics/employment/commuting/guidance/calculations.html.

commuting.work_elsewhere_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers who live in a municipio, how many work in another one.
commuting.work_elsewhere_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras que viven en un municipio, cuántas trabajan en otro.
commuting.work_elsewhere_pct.definition: Of the workers 16 and over who live in the municipio and work in Puerto Rico, the share whose workplace is in another municipio, in percent.
commuting.work_elsewhere_pct.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 and divides the workers who live in the municipio and work in another municipio by all the workers who live in it and work in Puerto Rico. The workers who work outside Puerto Rico are left out of both, as on the Connections between municipios page, whose figure this is. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion, with the margin of each sum as the square root of the sum of the squares of its flows' margins. It is a calculated figure (decision 107).
commuting.work_elsewhere_pct.how_to_read: In Puerto Rico, 53.4% of the workers who work on the island work in a municipio other than the one where they live (margin ±0.46). The share is highest in Toa Alta (87.5%), Loíza (82.8%) and Canóvanas (78.5%), and lowest in the island municipios of Vieques (2.7%) and Culebra (3.8%), then Ponce (15.4%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 4 of the 78 municipalities.
caveats: The Connections between municipios page gives 53.3% for Puerto Rico because it divides by all workers, including those who work outside Puerto Rico.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020.

population.acs_disability_pct.plain: Out of every 100 people the survey counts outside institutions, how many have a disability.
population.acs_disability_pct.definition: People with a disability divided by the civilian population living outside institutions (table B18101: the six age groups with a disability, male and female, over the total), in percent. The survey asks about hearing, vision, cognitive, walking, self-care and independent-living difficulty.
population.acs_disability_pct.method: The observatory reads table B18101 (Sex by Age by Disability Status) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the twelve cells "With a disability" (004, 007, 010, 013, 016, 019, 023, 026, 029, 032, 035, 038) and dividing by the total (001). The Census Bureau does not publish this table for block groups, so there is no block-group value. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_disability_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 22.9% of the civilian population of Puerto Rico living outside institutions has a disability. The share is highest in Aibonito (36.1%, ±2.5 points), Cidra (35.9%, ±1.8 points) and Rincón (33.4%, ±2.8 points) and lowest in Culebra (6.6%, ±4.7 points, less reliable). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 4% of municipalities, 45% of barrios and 17% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: In a very small area the share can read 0% or 100% from a handful of people, with a margin of hundreds of points: do not quote it (methods.small_area_estimates says how many areas are that small).
It counts difficulties as people report them in a survey; it is not a count of the people who receive disability benefits or services.
People living in institutions (nursing homes, prisons) are not in the table, so an area with an institution reads differently from its surroundings.
Below the municipality the figure is a rough survey estimate: read it with its margin of error and see methods.small_area_estimates for how large the margins are.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

population.acs_veteran_pct.method: The observatory reads table B21001 (Sex by Age by Veteran Status for the Civilian Population 18 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by dividing the veterans (002) by the civilian population 18 and older (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_veteran_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 2.4% of the civilian adults of Puerto Rico are veterans. The share is highest in Culebra (5.2%, ±4.2 points, less reliable), Ceiba (4.1%, ±1.4 points, less reliable) and Fajardo (4.1%, ±0.8 points); a margin above 30% of the estimate is what the site calls less reliable, so these are not firm rankings. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 62% of municipalities, 98% of barrios and 100% of census tracts that have a value.

layers.hex_grid.plain: A map layer of equal hexagons of 1 km² over the island, shaded by residents, housing units, buildings, land under buildings or residents in the flood area, to compare places below the barrio in one unit.
layers.hex_grid.plain_es: Una capa del mapa de hexágonos iguales de 1 km² sobre la isla, sombreada por residentes, unidades de vivienda, edificios, suelo ocupado por edificios o residentes en el área de inundación, para comparar lugares por debajo del barrio en una misma unidad.
layers.hex_grid.definition: hex_grid.geojson: 8,745 hexagons of 1 km² (6,887 with residents), each with p (residents, 2020 Census), h (housing units), b (buildings), bf (land under buildings, % of the hexagon) and pf (residents in FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, % of the hexagon's residents). The hexagons add up to Puerto Rico's 3,285,874 residents, 1,598,159 housing units and 2,157,363 buildings.
layers.hex_grid.method: hexgrid.py lays the map's own equal-area hexagons (core/hexbin.js: a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centered on Puerto Rico, pointy-topped hexagons of exactly 1 km²) and counts in each the census blocks by their internal point and the building footprints by their point. A block is counted whole in one hexagon, so a count per hexagon is calculated, not spread: a large rural block puts all its residents in one hexagon. A block is in the flood area when its internal point is (exposure.py's rule). Equal area means a count per hexagon is also a density per km².
layers.hex_grid.how_to_read: Pick the measure under the layer. Because every hexagon is 1 km², the shades compare density directly. Read a single rural hexagon with care: a census block can be larger than a hexagon. The hexagons are not the FCC's H3 hexagons of the broadband layer, which vary in area.
caveats: A census block is counted whole in the hexagon of its internal point; a block that spans several hexagons puts all its residents in one.
Buildings include sheds and other small structures in the footprint data.
Residents in the flood area use FEMA's 1% annual chance area as published in flood.geojson (outlines simplified by about 5 m).
layers.hex_grid.geography: Hexagons over Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra
layers.hex_grid.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); Overture Maps buildings, release 2026-10-21.0; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (flood.geojson)

population.acs_family_households_pct.definition: Family households divided by all households of the area (table B11001, cell 002 over cell 001), in percent. A family household has a householder (the person in whose name the home is owned or rented) living with one or more relatives by birth, marriage or adoption.
population.acs_family_households_pct.method: The observatory reads table B11001 (Household Type (Including Living Alone)) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by dividing the family households (002) by all households (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_family_households_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 63.4% of the households of Puerto Rico are family households (margin ±0.32 points). The share is highest in Toa Alta (73.9%) and lowest in San Juan (50.8%). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 0% of municipalities, 23% of barrios and 3% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: A household is a home with people in it; the number of households is not the number of homes (housing.housing_units includes the empty ones).

housing.avg_household_size.plain: The average number of people living in each home where people live. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.avg_household_size.plain_es: El número promedio de personas que viven en cada vivienda ocupada. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.avg_household_size.definition: People living in occupied housing units divided by the number of occupied housing units, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25010. People in group housing are not counted.
housing.avg_household_size.method: ACS 5-year table B25010 (Average Household Size of Occupied Housing Units by Tenure), cell 001 (all occupied housing units), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it, with two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in people per household.
housing.avg_household_size.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide average falls from 3.03 in 2006-2010 to 2.48 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.01). In 2020-2024 it runs from 2.12 (Guayama) to 3.15 (Naranjito). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: It is not residents per housing unit (housing.residents_per_unit), which also divides by empty homes and counts people in group housing.
It is an average, so it hides the mix of one-person and large households.
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 13% of barrios, less than 1% of census tracts and 10% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

housing.households.plain: The estimated number of homes where people live. Each occupied home is one household. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.households.plain_es: El número estimado de viviendas ocupadas. Cada vivienda ocupada es un hogar. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.households.definition: Occupied housing units, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25003. A household is all the people who live in one housing unit, so households and occupied units are the same count.
housing.households.method: ACS 5-year table B25003 (Tenure), cell 001 (all occupied housing units), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct.plain: Out of every 100 people aged 5 or older, how many say they speak English less than "very well".
population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas de 5 años o más, cuántas dicen que hablan inglés menos que "muy bien".
population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct.definition: People 5 and older who speak a language other than English at home and rate their English as "well", "not well" or "not at all", divided by all people 5 and older (table B16004), in percent. It is 100 minus the share who speak only English at home or rate their English as "very well".
population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct.method: The observatory reads table B16004 (Age by Language Spoken at Home by Ability to Speak English for the Population 5 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows. It adds the 15 cells of people who speak only English at home or speak English "very well" (in each of the three age groups, the cell "Speak only English" and the cell 'Speak English "very well"' of each of the four language groups), divides by the total (001) and takes that share from 100. The complement of a share has the margin of error of the share. The Census Bureau does not publish block-group values here. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 74.9% of the people of Puerto Rico aged 5 or older speak English less than "very well" (margin ±0.27), against 75.9% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Guaynabo (57.4%), Dorado (62.9%) and Bayamón (66.1%); it is highest in Maricao (93.5%), Las Marías (89.3%) and Naranjito (89.0%). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the map hatches such values and the CSV by area marks them as less reliable) for 0% of municipalities, 10% of barrios and less than 1% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: It is each person's own rating of their English, not a test. It says nothing about Spanish: in 2020-2024, 95.3% of the people of Puerto Rico aged 5 or older speak Spanish at home.

netmig_age.netmig_10_plus_pct.plain: How many people aged 10 and over in 2020 each municipio gained or lost to migration since 2010, per 100 it would have had with no migration.
netmig_age.netmig_10_plus_pct.plain_es: Cuántas personas de 10 o más años en 2020 ganó o perdió cada municipio por la migración desde 2010, por cada 100 que habría tenido sin migración.
netmig_age.netmig_10_plus_pct.definition: Net migration between the 2010 and 2020 censuses of the people aged 10 and over in 2020 (aged 0 to over in 2010), per 100 of the people of that age the municipio would have had with no migration: positive, more came than left; negative, more left. An estimate by the residual method: the 2020 census count of each age group minus the survivors of the same people in the 2010 census, by sex, with Puerto Rico's life table (UN World Population Prospects 2024, 2010-2019). It counts moves to and from the rest of Puerto Rico and abroad together, net; errors in either census land in it, and in small municipios a few hundred people can move the figure.
netmig_age.netmig_10_plus_pct.method: netmig_age.py compares, for each municipio, sex and five-year age group, the people aged a to a+4 in the 2010 census with the same generation, aged a+10 to a+14, in the 2020 census. Puerto Rico's life table (UN World Population Prospects 2024, the person-years lived by age and sex averaged over 2010-2019) says how many of them would still be alive; the 2020 count minus those survivors is the net migration of the group. Children under 10 in 2020, born during the decade, are left out.
netmig_age.netmig_10_plus_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: -11.3%. Lowest: Guánica (-28.0%), Maricao (-25.0%), Loíza (-22.8%). Highest: Rincón (3.2%), Culebra (-0.3%), Hormigueros (-4.4%). Range for the island, ages 10 and over: -362,347 with the life table of 2010 alone, -406,137 with that of 2019.
caveats: Net: people who moved within Puerto Rico and people who left for or came from abroad are counted together, and arrivals cancel departures.
College towns show a loss in the ages that were students in 2010: the census counts students where they study (Mayagüez's university, for one), and most leave after graduating.
Errors in either census land in the estimate, and the 2020 census added noise to protect privacy: in small municipios a few hundred people move a rate by several points.
One life table for the whole island: a municipio where people die younger than average shows a little more out-migration than it had.

Check: the residual for every age (ages 10 and over, -384,100, plus about -44,868 children born in the decade) is -428,968, 6.1% from the demographic balance of the two censuses (-456,866: the change in population minus births plus deaths). The UN's net migration for 2010-2019 is -408,407; the Census Bureau's estimate made before the 2020 census, -583,765, overstated the loss.

population.age_table.method: small_area.py (age_file) reads tables B01001 (Sex by Age) and B09001 (Population Under 18 Years by Age) for every window and level through acs_small.py. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. municipalities.pop_change_pct.plain: How much the population grew or shrank between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses, as a percent of the 2010 population. Between those two counts, every municipality lost people.

municipalities.pop_change_pct.definition: (population_2020 minus population_2010) divided by population_2010, times 100, rounded to one decimal. A value of -13.4 means the population fell by 13.4% over the ten years.
municipalities.pop_change_pct.method: Calculated in build.py from the two census counts of the same municipality.
municipalities.pop_change_pct.how_to_read: It is a ten-year change, not a yearly rate. Between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses all 78 values are negative, from -29.0 (Guánica) to -0.1 (Rincón); Maricao (-24.2) and Loíza (-21.2) follow Guánica. Taken together, the 78 municipalities fell from 3,725,789 to 3,285,874 people, which is -11.8% (worked out from the municipal values, not stored in the file). San Juan went from 395,326 to 342,259 people, which is -13.4%. In the 3D view, taller and redder columns mean bigger losses, because every value is a loss.
caveats: It shows how many fewer or more residents were counted. It does not say why: births, deaths and moves are not separated.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Housing page's 2020 population uses the Census Bureau's updated April 2020 base, so its change since 2010 differs from this field by 0.1 percentage point or less (for example Corozal, -7.0 there and -6.9 here).

housing.median_age.plain: The age that splits residents in half: half are younger and half are older. There is one value, in years, for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.median_age.plain_es: La edad que divide a las personas residentes en dos mitades: la mitad es más joven y la otra mitad es mayor. Hay un valor, en años, para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.median_age.definition: Median age of all residents, in years, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B01002.
housing.median_age.method: ACS 5-year table B01002 (Median Age by Sex), cell 001 (both sexes), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it, with one decimal. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in years.
housing.median_age.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide median age rises from 35.9 in 2006-2010 to 44.8 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.2 years). In 2020-2024 it runs from 40.0 (Naguabo) to 50.2 (Hormigueros). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.
On the Analysis tab the margin of error of median age prints as '± ... pts', but it is in years (see measures.margin_of_error).

It comes from the survey, while the share aged 65 and over (housing.age65_pct) comes from the Census Bureau's population estimates. They measure different things, a middle value and a share, so the two need not move together.
A median does not show the spread: a place with many children and many older adults can have the same median as a place of middle-aged adults.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 23% of barrios, 5% of census tracts and 35% of block groups that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty. See methods.small_area_estimates.

housing.pop_change_since_2010_pct.plain: How much the population has changed since the April 2010 census, as a percent, for each year from 2011 up to the latest (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). A negative value means fewer people live there than in 2010.
housing.pop_change_since_2010_pct.plain_es: Cuánto ha cambiado la población desde el Censo de abril de 2010, en por ciento, para cada año desde 2011 hasta el más reciente (2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Un valor negativo significa que allí viven menos personas que en 2010.
housing.pop_change_since_2010_pct.definition: Population in the selected year minus the 2010 census count, divided by the 2010 census count, times 100. Values exist for each year from 2011 to the latest vintage year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.pop_change_since_2010_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py from the population variable (housing.population): (population in the year - population in 2010) / population in 2010 x 100, rounded to two decimals. The 2010 population is the census count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for 2011-2019 the numerator is a Vintage 2020 estimate (the 2020 release of the Census Bureau's yearly estimates, built on the 2010 census); for 2020-2025 it is the 2020 base or a Vintage 2025 estimate (built on the 2020 census). There is no value for 2010 itself. The data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for example -11.8% for Puerto Rico in 2020).
housing.pop_change_since_2010_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide change is -11.81% in 2020 and -14.52% in 2025. In 2025 only one of the 78 municipalities, Rincón (+2.51%), has more people than in 2010; in 2020 none did. The largest losses in 2025 are Guánica (-39.05%) and Maricao (-30.91%). The Housing page shades the map around zero. Each year's 'basis' label in housing_series.json is one of those listed under Codes in housing.population.
caveats: The series steps back up in 2020 because the 2011-2019 estimates were not revised to the 2020 census count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide value is -14.29% for 2019 and -11.81% for 2020. Read 2011-2019 and 2020-2025 as two stretches, and use the 2020 value for the census-to-census comparison. Only the island population chart on the Housing page marks this break; the profile trend line, the full-data chart and the CSV download do not (the full-data panel states the break in a note above the table).
The same number of people is a larger percent in a small municipality. Check the count in housing.population before comparing places of different size.
The base date is April 1, 2010 and later values are July 1, so the 2011 value spans 15 months, not one year.
municipalities.json:pop_change_pct is the 2010-to-2020 census change rounded to one decimal. It differs from this variable's 2020 value by at most 0.1 point.
These values rest on population estimates, and the Census Bureau's estimate files have no margin-of-error column.

housing.population.plain: How many people live in the municipality, for each year from 2010 to the latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2010 and 2020 values are for April 1. All other years are Census Bureau estimates for July 1. Estimates before 2020 rest on the 2010 census and later ones on the 2020 census, so do not read 2019 to 2020 as one year of growth.
housing.population.plain_es: Cuántas personas viven en el municipio, para cada año desde 2010 hasta el más reciente (2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Los valores de 2010 y 2020 son al 1 de abril. Los demás años son estimados del Negociado del Censo al 1 de julio. Los estimados antes de 2020 se basan en el Censo de 2010 y los posteriores en el Censo de 2020, así que el cambio de 2019 a 2020 no debe leerse como un año de crecimiento.
housing.population.definition: People who usually live in the municipality, including people in group housing such as dormitories and care homes. The 2010 value is the April 1, 2010 census count. The 2020 value is for April 1, 2020: it is the base of the latest estimates, which is close to but not always equal to the census count (see the Cautions). All other years are the Census Bureau's population estimates for July 1. A vintage is one annual release of estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2011-2019 come from Vintage 2020 (built on the 2010 census) and 2021-2025 come from Vintage 2025 (built on the 2020 census).
housing.population.method: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the values are read from two Census Bureau files. 2010 and 2011-2019: PRM-EST2020.csv, columns CENSUS2010POP and POPESTIMATE2011 to POPESTIMATE2019. 2020 and 2021-2025: cc-est2025-agesex-72.csv, column POPESTIMATE (YEAR 1 is the April 1, 2020 base; YEAR 3 to 7 are July 1, 2021 to 2025). The July 1, 2020 estimate in the same file (YEAR 2) is not used. The island total for 2010-2019 is the Census Bureau's island row; for 2020 on it is the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the same snapshot, the island total equals the sum of the 78 municipalities in every year.
housing.population.how_to_read: This is a level: it says how many people live in a place, not how fast the place is changing. To see change, compare 2010 with 2020 (two census-based values), or compare years inside one base (2011-2019, or 2020-2025). Do not read the difference between 2019 and 2020 as one year of growth. In housing_series.json each year also carries a 'basis' label that says which of these it is (listed under Codes).
caveats: The series steps up in 2020. The Census Bureau built the 2011-2019 estimates on the 2010 census and did not revise them to match the 2020 census, so the two stretches rest on different counts. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide July 2019 estimate is 3,193,553 and the 2020 value is 3,285,874, a rise of 92,321 people (2.9%). By municipality the step runs from -13.7% (Gurabo) to +16.0% (Lares); 51 municipalities step up and 27 step down. The island population chart on the Housing page marks the change of base with a dashed line. The profile trend lines, the full-data chart and the CSV (comma-separated values) download do not (the full-data panel states the break in a note above the table), so treat 2019 to 2020 as a break there too.

The 2020 value is the April 1, 2020 base of the Vintage 2025 estimates, not the original census file. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it differs by 1 to 31 people from the 2020 census count in 68 of the 78 municipalities (the census count is from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb map service, 2020 counties layer, field POP100, the total number of residents, stored in municipalities.json:population_2020). The island total is the same in both, 3,285,874. The data files and the Housing page label this value 'census count'; read that label as the April 1, 2020 base described here.

The 2023 study prints 3,285,694 for Puerto Rico in 2020, which is 180 fewer than this variable's 3,285,874 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Cite this variable's figure for Census Bureau data and the study's figure only for the study's own table (see study.table_2).

The base date is April 1, 2020 and later values are July 1, so the change from 2020 to 2021 spans 15 months and the change to 2025 spans 5 years and 3 months. Do not read the 2021 value as one year of change, and do not divide a change by a number of years without using the real dates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Census Bureau's July 1, 2020 island estimate (3,281,591) is in the same file, but this variable does not use it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2011-2019 estimates show the island falling 4.0% between July 2017 and July 2018 (3,325,284 to 3,193,344), a period that includes Hurricane Maria (September 2017), and then staying flat in 2019 (+209 people). The data do not show the cause.

Cite the vintage with the figure. In the 2026-10 snapshot this file uses Vintage 2020 for 2010-2019 and Vintage 2025 for 2020-2025. The Census Bureau says the latest vintage replaces earlier estimates for the same dates, so the 2021-2025 values can change when the observatory loads a newer vintage.
Apart from the 2010 census count, these are estimates, not head counts. The Census Bureau's population estimate files have no margin-of-error column.
The American Community Survey also estimates population (table B01003). This variable does not use it, so the two can differ.

exposure.total.plain: The number of residents and the number of housing units of each municipio, barrio and census tract in the 2020 Census, repeated in each exposure file so a share can be worked out from the file alone.
exposure.total.plain_es: La cantidad de residentes y de unidades de vivienda de cada municipio, barrio y sector censal en el Censo de 2020. Se repite en cada archivo de exposición para poder calcular una proporción solo con ese archivo.
exposure.total.definition: The total field of each exposure file holds two lists, pop and hu, one value for each area in the order of geo.ids: the 2020 Census residents and housing units of the area, the sum of its census blocks. They equal the geography crosswalk's values. For the whole island, 3,285,874 residents and 1,598,159 housing units.
exposure.total.method: Copied from the crosswalk's pop and hu (geo.py), after the build has checked that the blocks add up to them for every area.
exposure.total.how_to_read: Divide an exposure count by the matching total to get a share. Counts add up between levels; shares do not.

methods.wcrp_rvi.plain: How the WCRP vulnerability index ranks barrios: each input becomes a percentile among barrios, the percentiles of an area are added and ranked again, the six areas are added for the overall index, and levels are fifths.
methods.wcrp_rvi.plain_es: Cómo el índice de vulnerabilidad WCRP ordena los barrios: cada variable se convierte en un percentil entre barrios, los percentiles de un área se suman y se ordenan otra vez, las seis áreas se suman para el índice general y los niveles son quintos.
methods.wcrp_rvi.definition: Hunter College built the Risk and Vulnerability Indicators (RVI) for Foundation for Puerto Rico's Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program (white paper, December 2021; data published March 2022). Steps: (1) each input becomes a percentile among the barrios with a value, higher meaning more vulnerable; (2) within an area the percentiles are added and the sum ranked again (infrastructure through two sub-indicators; the white paper describes two for housing too, but the published housing index is the plain sum of its inputs); (3) the overall index ranks the sum of the six area indices with equal weights; (4) ranks are fifths: 1 = 0 to 0.20 (low) to 5 = above 0.80 (high). Barrios with no residents have no value; in education, 21 barrios with nobody aged 3 to 24 have their no-diploma percentile doubled. The observatory shows the original as published and a rebuild on ACS 2020–2024 and its current local conditions (conditions_barrio.json). Input left out of the rebuild: Solid waste facilities (transfer stations, recycling, open dumps) (environment).
methods.wcrp_rvi.method: The percentile that reproduces the original from its own inputs is the share of barrios with a strictly lower value (n = barrios with a value). With it, the original's own inputs give back its published index with rank correlation 1.00 for overall, education, health, housing and infrastructure; economy (0.68) and environment (0.93) do not reproduce. Housing reproduces as a flat sum of its three inputs (1.00), not as the two sub-indicators the white paper describes (0.96). A hypothesis to confirm with Hunter College: the published economy index matches one built from public assistance, poverty and per capita income, with higher income counted as more vulnerable and without unemployment, much better (rank correlation 0.93, 81% same rank). Where the rebuild differs: ranking the original's 2015-2019 values with the rebuild's inputs changes 29% of overall ranks (almost all through economy and environment); the rebuild changes the overall rank of 68% of the 879 barrios ranked in both and moves 29% two ranks or more; the rebuild on 2017-2021 and on 2020-2024, with the same non-survey inputs, differs for 52% of barrios. tests/test_wcrp_rvi.py checks the method on a small hand-worked example.
methods.wcrp_rvi.how_to_read: A rank is relative: it says which fifth of barrios a place falls in on the inputs used, not how much need there is.
caveats: A rank compares barrios with each other on the inputs used. It is not a measure of need, risk of harm or eligibility for any program.

Foundation for Puerto Rico runs WCRP in collaboration with the Puerto Rico Department of Housing (PRDOH), with HUD CDBG-DR funds. The WCRP page is published with an 'In review' marker: these values may change, and the page asks search engines not to index it while the marker is on.
Hazards (flood, landslide, sea level rise) are not inputs, as the white paper decided.
